items.User: You are a senior game systems engineer specializing in retro-modern arcade flight simulators. Your task is to design and implement the core gameplay architecture for a spiritual successor to 1989's F29 Retaliator. Unlike modern realistic simulators (like DCS), this game prioritizes pure arcade action: aircraft have infinite missile/weapon payloads (governed by cooldown timers rather than inventory counts) and enemy waves are endless or dynamically respawning to maintain non-stop dogfighting tension.

Agent.text: All checks pass. Refreshing the browser build with the latest code and recording what's still open.

I built "Strike Vector", an arcade jet-combat game that runs on a computer and in a web browser, including on phones. You fly from a cockpit with a green heads-up display. The gun and three kinds of missile never run out and only wait on cooldown timers, and enemy fighters, aces and ground targets keep coming in endless waves. On a phone you tilt it to steer and use on-screen buttons to fire the gun, launch missiles, switch missiles and drop flares, with a slider for throttle. A LEVEL button re-centres the tilt, and if the phone has no tilt sensor you can drag on the left side of the screen to steer instead.

- **Checks:** the build, screenshot and self-test all passed. I also loaded the browser version in a test browser and it starts and draws.
- **Not tested on a real phone:** I had no phone here. The tilt direction is my best guess (rocking the top edge toward you climbs), and the pause screen has a switch to flip it if it feels backwards.
- **Hosting:** phones only allow the tilt sensor on secure (https) web pages, so the browser version has to be put on an https site before it works on a phone.
- **Not matched to the original:** the flight, weapon and enemy numbers are my own estimates, the look is an original design because there were no pictures of the original to compare, and the game has no sound yet.

Next, you could try it on your phone and tell me whether the tilt feels right, or ask for engine and missile sounds.

Agent.text: The game is now called Retal, and the title, pause and game-over screens let you choose Easy, Normal or Hard (tap a box or press Left/Right). Easy makes the enemy pilots slower, weaker and worse shots, and makes your weapons easier to use: faster missile locks, shorter cooldowns, gun aim help, and missiles that chase a target before the lock is complete. Hard does the opposite and Normal sits in between. The radar missile is now selected at the start of every flight, the browser version is rebuilt, and all checks pass. Two limits remain: the difficulty choice resets each time the game is reopened, and the numbers are still my own estimates rather than the original's.

Agent.text:
I decided that the host picks the match type when creating it: **Co-op** (everyone teams up against the endless enemy waves) or **Dogfight** (players shoot each other while the enemy bots keep flying), so either way of playing together is covered.

There's now a Multiplayer button on the title screen. You create a named match and make it public (anyone can join from the match list) or private (players need the password, or the 4-letter code plus the password). Up to 8 players fit in a match, everyone respawns endlessly, and the pause menu shows a scoreboard and a leave button.

The game's automatic test now plays a whole match on this computer, and all checks pass. In it a wrong password is refused, a guest joins with the right one, sees the host's enemies and can shoot them down for points, a public match lets anyone in, and one player shoots another down in Dogfight.

- **A shared server is needed:** everyone has to reach the same small Retal server program, which also serves the browser version. The desktop game starts one by itself on your computer when none is running, which is enough for players on the same home network.
- **Not tested:** I haven't tried real phones or players in different places over the internet. For that the server has to run on a computer everyone can reach, with a secure (https) address so phone tilt still works.
- **Limits:** a match ends when its host leaves, and pilot names aren't remembered between sessions.
- **One test froze once:** the automatic test stalled one time early on and finished normally in the nine runs after that; I didn't find the cause.

A good next step would be help putting the server online so friends anywhere can join.

Agent.text:
The game now builds into a `public-html` folder that works as a plain static website, for example on GitHub Pages. I tested it served from a sub-folder, the way GitHub Pages serves a project site. A short guide and an example GitHub Pages publishing file are in the `deploy` folder; to use the publishing file you copy it to `.github/workflows/` at the top of your repository, which sits outside the game folder.

For phones, I took your extra note into account:
- **Tilt steering:** it's smoother now and re-levels automatically when the phone is turned. The title screen says whether the tilt sensor is on or blocked.
- **Sensitivity:** the pause screen has a Low / Normal / High tilt setting.
- **Smoother play:** phones draw a shorter, foggier view so the game runs more smoothly.
- **Screen and notch:** the screen stays on while you play, and the game area keeps clear of the notch.
- **Home screen:** it can be added to the home screen as a full-screen app with its own icon.

I haven't tried it on a real phone, so how the tilt feels in your hands is still untested.

Multiplayer can't run on a static host by itself. Solo play works fully, but to play together you need the separate Retal match server running somewhere, with a secure (wss://) address entered once in `config.js` or typed in the lobby. Each device remembers the last address that worked.

The automatic self-test failed once this turn by running past 90 seconds, probably because the game window was covered and drew slowly. I changed it to run several game steps per drawn frame; it now finishes in under a second, and all checks pass.
